newsitem.title: USA: Brokers to meet, celebrate record year.
newsitem.headline: Brokers to meet, celebrate record year.

text.p: Hundreds of executives from brokers and investment houses flew to Boca Raton, Fla., Tuesday, prepared to congratulate each other on another record year for Wall Street.

But those attending the annual meeting of the Securities Industry Association, which runs Wednesday through Saturday, are not likely to focus on the rear-view mirror for long. They were set to discuss a host of regulatory issues on the horizon and, of course, the impact of the elections.
Participants like New York Stock Exchange Chairman Richard Grasso and Securities and Exchange Commission Chairman Arthur Levitt will be the focus of many an exeuctive's attention.

"It's important to listen to what non-industry members like Grasso and anybody from the SEC have to say," said Perrin Long, an independent analyst covering securities firms. "What they say can have long-term implications for the industry."
The meeting, which ends on Saturday, will no doubt devote some attention to the undeniable industry successes of 1996, such as the record pace of mergers and initial public offerings.
Merger and acquisition activity is booming, with the association estimating total deal volume for 1996 at about $496 billion, nearly triple 1993 levels.
Of course, many will question whether the industry can duplicate its results next year, and at least one panel will discuss the outlook for the economy and markets.

Panellists will include Abby Joseph Cohen, co-chair of Goldman Sachs & Co.'s investment policy committee, Gail Dudack, chief investment strategist at UBS Securities, and Byron Wein, Morgan Stanley's top U.S. investment strategist.
"Mini-conferences" during the meeting will address securities legislation and regulation, as well as federal fiscal and tax policy. A panel discussion of the 1996 election results is also scheduled.
Technology will also occupy centre stage, as securities and technology executives explore topics like the growing use of the Internet for brokerage and research distribution.

Featured technology executives will include Henry Schacht, chairman of Lucent Technologies Inc., the maker of telecommunications gear recently spun off by AT&T Corp., and Scott Cook, chairman of Intuit Inc., a maker of personal finance software.
Among this year's highlights, according to the association's figures, the 603 initial public offerings through September alone exceeded 1995's figure by 5 percent.
The annualized rate of initial offerings of $46.9 billion was 56 percent higher than 1995's total and 13 percent higher than 1993's record amount.
